pos: n. (the Yorkshire Benedictine abbey founded about 1069, whose church survives whole as a parish church)
etymology: From Old Norse selja, a willow, with by, a settlement; the willow village on the Ouse.
biblical_def: Selby Abbey stands on the Ouse below York, founded about 1069 by a monk named Benedict from Auxerre who claimed a vision directing him to a place marked by three swans, and endowed by William the Conqueror, who was then in Yorkshire burning it. It was the first Benedictine house founded in the north after the Conquest, grew rich on the Ouse trade, and its abbot was one of only two in the north to be mitred. At the Dissolution the monastery was suppressed and the great church, unusually, was kept; it was bought for the parish, survived a fire in 1906 that gutted it, and was rebuilt. Its Norman nave and the east window remain. The dictionary records Selby for its founding story, which turns on a vow. Benedict vowed to build where the vision sent him and did it, and monastic life was constructed entirely on vows of that kind, which is the point at which Scripture has something severe to say. A vow is not a devotional ornament; it is a debt, and the warning is that it is better not to vow at all than to vow and not pay.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vow as a solemn promise made to God; to pay as to discharge a debt; to defer as to put off; to slack as to be remiss; and to require as to demand as of right.
webster_full: VOW, n. A solemn promise made to God, or by a pagan to his deity; a promise by which one binds himself to an act, service or condition.
PAY, v.t. To discharge a debt; to deliver to a creditor the value of what is due to him; to fulfil, as a promise.
DEFER, v.t. To delay; to put off; to postpone to a future time; to procrastinate.
SLACK, a. Not tense; not hard drawn; remiss; not holding fast; weak; not earnest or eager.
REQUIRE, v.t. To demand; to ask as of right and by authority; to claim as by right; to exact.
corruption_summary: Yorkshire Benedictine abbey founded about 1069 on the strength of a monk's vision and vow, whose church survived the Dissolution as a parish church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the seriousness of a vow, which Scripture treats as a contracted debt rather than a pious gesture. The Preacher gives the command and the reason together: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools” (Ecc 5:4), and then the safer counsel for anyone inclined to promise freely, “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5).

The live temptation in monastic religion was to multiply vows and then to administer them, dispensing, commuting and selling relief from obligations men had taken on themselves. The law allows no such machinery: “When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee” (Deu 23:21). Where vows are made rightly they belong with worship and not with bargaining: “Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God” (Psa 76:11). Selby's founder paid his; the system built on such promises did not keep them so well.

pos: n. (the Yorkshire Cistercian abbey founded in 1132, the first in the north, ruled by Aelred and holding some six hundred men)
etymology: Norman French Rie vallis, the valley of the Rye, latinised Rievallis; the English pronunciation is a local survival.
biblical_def: Rievaulx was planted in a narrow valley of the Rye in the North York Moors in 1132 by twelve monks sent from Clairvaux by Bernard himself, and it was the first Cistercian house in the north of England. Under Aelred, abbot from 1147 to 1167, it held about one hundred and forty choir monks and five hundred lay brothers, and the lay brothers are the point: the Cistercian reform was an attempt to put monks back to manual work, clearing, draining, herding and smithing, instead of leaving the labour to tenants while the choir sang. Rievaulx ran enormous sheep flocks, mined and smelted iron, and diverted the river three times to get room to build. Aelred wrote the Mirror of Charity and On Spiritual Friendship and governed with a gentleness his biographer thought remarkable. The dictionary records Rievaulx for the dignity it gave to work. Scripture had settled the question long before: whatever is done is to be done heartily as to the Lord, whatever the hand finds to do is to be done with all one's might, and the man who will not work is not to eat.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines labor as bodily exertion; heartily as with sincerity and zeal; might as strength and power; service as the act of serving; and to work as to be employed in labor.
webster_full: LABOR, n. Exertion of muscular strength, or bodily exertion which occasions weariness; toil; work.
HEARTILY, adv. From the heart; with all the heart; with sincerity; really; cordially; with zeal.
MIGHT, n. Strength; force; power; ability; the power of doing or effecting any thing.
SERVICE, n. The act of serving; labor performed for another; office of a servant; duty done for another.
WORK, v.i. To labor; to be occupied in performing manual labor, whether severe or moderate.
corruption_summary: First Cistercian house in northern England, founded 1132 from Clairvaux, ruled by Aelred, with five hundred lay brothers doing its manual work.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that ordinary labour is service rendered to Christ and not a lower grade of life. Paul states it to slaves and so leaves nobody out: “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). The Preacher adds urgency from the shortness of life, “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might” (Ecc 9:10).

The live temptation, which the Cistercian reform existed to correct, is a two-tier religion in which prayer is holy and work is tolerated, with the work pushed onto other men. Paul will not have idleness dressed as devotion and made it a standing rule in Thessalonica: “that if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). The dignity he assigns to labour is explicit and it is the same for every station, “With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men” (Eph 6:7). Five hundred lay brothers draining a Yorkshire valley were doing divine service.

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey on the Wye, founded in 1131, the first Cistercian house in Wales)
etymology: Welsh Tyndyrn, the fort of the king, from din, a fort, and teyrn, a monarch.
biblical_def: Tintern Abbey stands in a bend of the Wye in Monmouthshire, founded in 1131 by Walter de Clare for Cistercians from Normandy, the second Cistercian house in Britain and the first in Wales. It was rebuilt on a grand scale in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries on the wealth of its granges and sheep, and its church, with the great west window and the long bare nave, is the most complete Cistercian ruin in Britain. The Black Death and the Welsh risings reduced it; it surrendered in 1536 and the lead was stripped from the roofs. From the 1770s it became the most visited ruin in the country, painted by Turner and written about by Wordsworth, and it taught the English to find a religious feeling in ruined abbeys without any religion in particular. The dictionary records Tintern for the exchange its history records. An order founded on poverty grew rich enough to build that church, and the church is now a landscape feature. Christ's instruction about treasure is not a counsel against prosperity but a statement about where moth, rust and thieves can reach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines treasure as wealth laid up; to corrupt as to waste and spoil; covetousness as an inordinate desire of gain; abundance as great plenty; and the root as the origin or cause.
webster_full: TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve; something very much valued.
CORRUPT, v.t. To change from a sound to a putrid state; to spoil; to waste; to consume; to vitiate.
COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good; avarice.
ABUNDANCE, n. Great plenty; an overflowing quantity; ample sufficiency; copiousness.
ROOT, n. That part of a plant which enters and fixes itself in the earth; the origin; the cause; the first ancestor.
corruption_summary: First Cistercian house in Wales, founded 1131 on the Wye, enriched by wool, stripped in 1536, and from the 1770s the most visited ruin in Britain.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ's reason for redirecting treasure, which is a plain fact about security rather than a hostility to property: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal” (Mat 6:19). The alternative is given in the same breath, “where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt” (Mat 6:20), and Tintern's stripped roofs are a demonstration of the first clause.

The live temptation is the aesthetic one that Tintern invented for the English, a reverence for the ruins of faith with no faith in it, which lets a man feel religious without being bound by anything. Christ's warning is to the man who thinks his life is measured by his holdings, “for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15). Paul diagnoses the slow failure of an order that began in poverty: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith” (1Ti 6:10).

pos: n. (the Wiltshire abbey of Aldhelm, and the house of William of Malmesbury, the best English historian after Bede)
etymology: Old English Maldumesburg, from the Irish hermit Maildub who settled there, with burh, a fortified place.
biblical_def: Malmesbury in Wiltshire grew round the cell of an Irish hermit called Maildub and became an abbey under Aldhelm, its abbot from about 675 and afterwards bishop of Sherborne, the first Englishman known to have written Latin verse and a letter-writer of ferocious learning. King Athelstan was buried there. Its greatest figure is William of Malmesbury, librarian of the house in the twelfth century, who travelled England collecting documents and wrote the Gesta Regum and Gesta Pontificum, the first serious attempt since Bede to write the history of the English and their church from the sources; he says plainly when he does not know something and when his authorities disagree. The abbey's nave survives as the parish church, with a carved porch. The dictionary records Malmesbury for William's method. The prophet is told to write the vision and make it plain, so that a man can read it running; the readers at Berea are commended for checking what they were told; and Nehemiah's Levites read distinctly and gave the sense. Clarity and verification are scriptural duties, not modern manners.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vision as something apparently seen otherwise than by ordinary sight; plain as evident and clear; to read as to utter written words; distinctly as clearly and without confusion; and to search as to examine carefully.
webster_full: VISION, n. The act of seeing external objects; something imaginary or supernaturally presented to the mind; a revelation.
PLAIN, a. Evident to the understanding; clear; manifest; not obscure or difficult; open; artless.
READ, v.t. To utter or pronounce written or printed words in the proper order; to peruse; to learn by observation.
DISTINCTLY, adv. Separately; with distinctness; clearly; plainly; without confusion of parts or sounds.
SEARCH, v.t. To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something; to examine; to explore.
corruption_summary: Wiltshire abbey of Aldhelm, later the house of William of Malmesbury, the first since Bede to write English church history from the sources.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that plainness and checkability are duties and not merely virtues of style. The LORD'S instruction to Habakkuk settles the standard: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). The Levites at the Water Gate met the same standard with a text, reading “in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense” (Neh 8:8).

The live temptation for a monastic historian was the house chronicle written to flatter its patrons and manufacture its charters, which many English abbeys produced and William of Malmesbury largely refused to produce. Luke commends the Bereans for the practice that makes such forgery unprofitable: they “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). And the willingness to be corrected is the mark of a wise man rather than a weak one, for “A wise man will hear, and will increase learning” (Pro 1:5).

pos: n. (the Devon town, birthplace of Boniface, and see of Devon and Cornwall from 909 until the bishop moved to Exeter in 1050)
etymology: Old English Cridiantun, the farm on the river Creedy, a British river name.
biblical_def: Crediton in mid Devon was the seat of the bishops of Devon, and after 994 of Devon and Cornwall together, from 909 until Leofric moved the see to the walled safety of Exeter in 1050; its great collegiate church survives. Its chief claim is that Wynfrith, who took the name Boniface, was born there about 675. He went from Wessex to the Frisians and then to the Germans, was made archbishop of Mainz, organised the church of Germany, crowned Pepin, and at Geismar in Hesse felled the oak sacred to Thunor in the presence of a hostile crowd, built a chapel from its timber, and was not struck down; the Hessians were converted in numbers after it. He was killed at Dokkum in 754 with a book raised over his head. The dictionary records Crediton for Geismar. Boniface's axe was an argument, and it was the argument the prophets had already made: that an idol is the work of men's hands, that it cannot do evil nor good, and that the Godhead is not like unto gold or silver or stone graven by art.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an idol as an image worshipped as a god; graven as carved and engraved; vanity as emptiness and worthlessness; a device as a contrivance; and offspring as children and descendants.
webster_full: IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship; a person or thing greatly loved.
GRAVEN, pp. Carved; engraved; cut with a chisel or other instrument on stone, wood or metal.
VANITY, n. Emptiness; want of substance to satisfy desire; emptiness of pretension; fruitless desire.
DEVICE, n. That which is formed by design; a contrivance; an invention; that which is fancied or imagined.
OFFSPRING, n. A child or children; a descendant or descendants, however remote from the stock.
corruption_summary: Devon town, see of Devon and Cornwall from 909 to 1050, and birthplace of Boniface, who felled the oak of Thunor at Geismar.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prophetic argument against idols, which is empirical before it is theological. Isaiah states the conclusion first: “They that make a graven image are all of them vanity” (Isa 44:9). Jeremiah presses the practical test that Boniface applied with an axe, that the thing cannot act: “Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:5).

The live temptation is subtler than wooden images and Paul names it at Athens, which is the assumption that God is of the same order as the material we would use to depict him: “we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device” (Act 17:29). John closes his epistle with the shortest form of the command, addressed to Christians and not to pagans: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jo 5:21). Boniface spent fifty years saying that, and the oak was one sentence of it.

pos: n. (Crowland in the Lincolnshire fens, the abbey built over the hermitage of Guthlac)
etymology: Old English Cruwland, the muddy or raw land, from cru, crude or raw, with land.
biblical_def: Croyland, now Crowland, is an island of slightly higher ground in the Lincolnshire fens, reached in Guthlac's time only by boat. Guthlac, a Mercian nobleman who had been a war leader, took the tonsure at Repton and about 699 went out to the fen to live alone in a robbed burial mound; the eighth-century life by Felix describes his years there in terms of a sustained conflict with devils and of visitors who came for counsel, Ethelbald of Mercia among them. An abbey was founded over his cell after his death in 714, burned by the Danes, rebuilt three times, and known in the Middle Ages for a cartulary of charters that were partly forged. Its triangular bridge and the ruined north aisle, still the parish church, remain. The dictionary records Croyland for the fen and the darkness. The Psalm that promises no fear of the terror by night or the pestilence that walks in darkness was the hermit's own psalm, and the gospel's own statement about darkness is that the light shines in it and the darkness has not put it out.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines terror as extreme fear; pestilence as a contagious disease; darkness as absence of light; to comprehend as to take in and seize; and light as that which makes objects visible.
webster_full: TERROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind; the cause of extreme fear.
PESTILENCE, n. Plague; pest; any contagious or infectious disease that is epidemic and mortal.
DARKNESS, n. Absence of light; obscurity; a state of being intellectually clouded; privacy; secrecy; wickedness.
COMPREHEND, v.t. To contain; to include; to comprise; to understand; to conceive; to seize or lay hold of.
LIGHT, n. That ethereal agent which makes objects visible; illumination of mind; instruction; knowledge; prosperity.
corruption_summary: Fenland abbey built over the hermitage of Guthlac, who went out to a burial mound in the Lincolnshire marsh about 699; rebuilt three times after Danish burning.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one promise a man alone in a marsh actually needs, and the Psalter gives it in the vocabulary of night and plague: “Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day” (Psa 91:5), and again, “Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness” (Psa 91:6). Guthlac's biographer describes exactly those fears and that confidence.

The live temptation with a hermit's legend is to make a drama of the devils and forget the verdict already pronounced on darkness. John states it as a finished fact with a present tense: “And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not” (Joh 1:5). And Paul applies the change to ordinary Christians rather than to spiritual athletes, reminding them what they were and what they now are: “For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light” (Eph 5:8). A fen is dark; the promise is not about the fen.

pos: n. (the fenland abbey founded in 969, a centre of the English monastic reform and of tenth-century learning)
etymology: Old English Hramesege, the island of wild garlic, from hramsa, ramsons, and eg, an island.
biblical_def: Ramsey Abbey was founded in 969 on a fen island by Ailwin, a kinsman of King Edgar, with Oswald, bishop of Worcester and afterwards archbishop of York, as its spiritual founder; it was one of the chief houses of the tenth-century English monastic revival alongside Ely, Peterborough and Thorney. Abbo of Fleury taught there for two years and wrote his life of Edmund from the testimony of an old man who had been the martyr's armour bearer; Byrhtferth of Ramsey wrote on computation and natural science. The abbey grew enormously rich on the fen, was dissolved in 1539, and its stone was carted off to build colleges at Cambridge. The dictionary records Ramsey for the question its wealth raises. A house endowed for learning and prayer accumulated more than it could use, and Scripture's teaching on giving is the standard by which such an endowment has to be judged: the tithe is brought into the storehouse so that there may be meat in God's house, the LORD is honoured with the firstfruits, the giver is to be cheerful, and the measure given is the measure received.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a tithe as the tenth part; a storehouse as a building for keeping grain or goods; firstfruits as the first produce offered to God; cheerful as lively and full of good spirits; and a measure as the standard of quantity.
webster_full: TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy for their support.
STOREHOUSE, n. A house in which things are stored; a magazine; a repository; a warehouse.
FIRSTFRUITS, n. The fruit or produce first matured and collected in any season; the first profits of any thing.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that giving to the house of God has a purpose stated in the command, which is provision and not accumulation. Malachi puts the purpose in the sentence: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house” (Mal 3:10), and Solomon fixes the order of a believer's money, “Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase” (Pro 3:9).

The live temptation on both sides of an endowment is visible at Ramsey. The abbey took more than it could spend and became a landlord; the crown then took the abbey and spent it. Paul describes the only giving God is said to love, and it is neither extracted nor grudged: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2Co 9:7). Christ attaches the reckoning to the giver's own standard, “For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again” (Luk 6:38), which is a warning to abbots and to kings alike.

pos: n. (the fen island abbey refounded in 972, whose church was later given to Huguenot and Walloon settlers to worship in French)
etymology: Old English Thorneg, the island of thorns, from thorn and eg, an island.
biblical_def: Thorney was a fen island in Cambridgeshire with an early hermitage, destroyed by the Danes and refounded as a Benedictine abbey in 972 by Ethelwold of Winchester as part of the monastic revival. It was never large, and at the Dissolution its church was reduced to the nave, which became the parish church. Its most interesting chapter came afterwards: when the Earl of Bedford drained the Great Level in the seventeenth century he brought in French-speaking Protestant refugees, Walloons and Huguenots skilled in dyke work, and they settled at Thorney in numbers. They were given the abbey church, a French minister was appointed, and services were held in French there from 1652 until 1727, with the registers kept in French. The dictionary records Thorney for that arrangement. A refugee congregation was received, housed and allowed to worship in its own language in an English parish church, which is what Scripture asks on both counts: strangers are to be entertained, and men are to hear in the tongue wherein they were born.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a stranger as a foreigner; to entertain as to receive and treat hospitably; a tongue as a language; to dwell as to abide as a resident; and richly as abundantly.
webster_full: STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; a guest; one not before known.
ENTERTAIN, v.t. To receive into the house and treat with hospitality, either at the table only, or with lodging also.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; a language; the whole sum of words used by a nation.
DWELL, v.i. To abide as a permanent resident, or to inhabit for a time; to live in a place; to have a habitation.
RICHLY, adv. With riches; with opulence; abundantly; plenteously; truly; really.
corruption_summary: Cambridgeshire fen abbey refounded in 972, whose surviving nave housed a French-speaking Huguenot and Walloon congregation from 1652 to 1727.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that receiving strangers is commanded, with a reason attached that leaves no room for calculation: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2). And what the strangers are to hear when they are received is their own speech, which is the plain marvel of Pentecost: “And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?” (Act 2:8).

The live temptation when refugees arrive with useful skills is to value the drainage and ignore the souls, or to require them to worship in the host's language as the price of a roof. Thorney did neither for seventy-five years. The aim in any language is the same: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16). And the host congregation had no higher standing than its guests, since Peter addresses every Christian in the terms the Walloons knew literally, “I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims” (1Pe 2:11).

pos: n. (the Worcestershire abbey founded about 701 on a swineherd's vision, and the battlefield of 1265)
etymology: Old English Eoveshamm, the river meadow of Eof, from the swineherd of the founding story and hamm, a water meadow.
biblical_def: Evesham Abbey in the Vale of Worcestershire was founded about 701 by Egwin, bishop of Worcester, on ground where, the house always said, a swineherd named Eof had seen a vision of the Virgin; the story put a herdsman at the head of the abbey's charter and the monks never dropped it. The abbey became one of the richest Benedictine houses in England. The battle of Evesham in 1265 was fought at its gates, Simon de Montfort was killed and dismembered, and his body was carried into the abbey church, where an unofficial cult grew up around his tomb that the crown spent years suppressing. Only the bell tower survived the Dissolution. The dictionary records Evesham for the vows and abstinences on which such a house was built, which is the point the Reformation pressed hardest. Paul calls the forbidding of marriage and the commanding of abstinence from meats a doctrine of devils; the writer to the Hebrews says marriage is honourable in all; and Christ himself dismissed the worship that teaches for doctrines the commandments of men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to forbid as to prohibit; to abstain as to refrain voluntarily; honourable as worthy of esteem; worship as adoration paid to a deity; and a commandment as a precept and order.
webster_full: FORBID, v.t. To prohibit; to interdict; to command to forbear or not to do; to oppose; to hinder.
ABSTAIN, v.i. To forbear or refrain from, voluntarily; particularly, to refrain from an indulgence of appetite.
HONORABLE, a. Worthy of honor; illustrious; noble; conferring honor; honest; without hypocrisy.
WORSHIP, n. Chiefly and eminently, the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being; adoration; religious reverence.
COMMANDMENT, n. A command; a mandate; an order or injunction given by authority; a precept.
corruption_summary: Rich Worcestershire abbey founded about 701 on a swineherd's vision, scene of the battle of 1265 and of an unofficial cult of Simon de Montfort.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that compulsory celibacy and compulsory abstinence are not higher forms of obedience, and Paul's language about them is deliberately harsh: he lists “Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3) among the marks of a departure from the faith. The writer to the Hebrews leaves no rank of Christians exempt from the honour he gives marriage: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4).

The live temptation is to grade Christians by their austerities, which Evesham's rule did by its nature and which Christ had already answered by quoting Isaiah at men who had done the same: “in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mar 7:7). Paul names the attractiveness of such rules and dismisses their power in one verse: they “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body” (Col 2:23). A great abbey and a saint's tomb at the gate were both built on that show.

pos: n. (the Gloucestershire abbey whose church the townsmen bought from the crown in 1543 and so preserved)
etymology: Old English Teodekesberie, the fortified place of Teoc, a hermit said to have settled at the meeting of the Severn and the Avon.
biblical_def: Tewkesbury Abbey stands where the Avon meets the Severn in Gloucestershire, refounded as a Benedictine house in 1102 and built on a scale to rival a cathedral, with the largest Norman tower in England and a ring of chantry chapels put up by the lords of Gloucester who were buried in it. The battle of Tewkesbury in 1471 ended the Lancastrian cause, and the Lancastrian leaders who took sanctuary in the abbey were dragged out and beheaded two days later. At the Dissolution in 1540 the monastery was suppressed and the church condemned; in 1543 the townsmen bought it from the crown for four hundred and fifty-three pounds, the valuation of its lead, bells and roof timber, and it has been the parish church since. The dictionary records Tewkesbury for that purchase, which was an assay. Men gave what they had for a building when nobody required them to, and Scripture describes God's dealings with his people in just that language: he sits as a refiner and purifier, he tries them as gold is tried, and the day declares every man's work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a refiner as one who purifies metal; to purge as to cleanse; to try as to prove by a test; gold as the most precious metal; and to declare as to make known.
webster_full: REFINER, n. One who refines metals; one who purifies any thing; an improver in purity and elegance.
PURGE, v.t. To cleanse or purify by separating and carrying off impurities, or whatever is superfluous.
TRY, v.t. To examine; to prove by a test; to purify or refine, as metals; to put to the proof.
GOLD, n. A precious metal of a bright yellow color, the heaviest of all metals except platinum; money; riches.
DECLARE, v.t. To make known; to tell explicitly; to manifest or communicate plainly; to publish.
corruption_summary: Gloucestershire abbey with the largest Norman tower in England, bought from the crown by the townsmen in 1543 for the value of its lead and bells.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's work with his people is described as assay rather than as reward. Malachi puts him at the furnace: “And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi” (Mal 3:3). Zechariah describes the same process applied to a remnant and its result, “and will try them as gold is tried: they shall call on my name, and I will hear them” (Zec 13:9).

The live temptation at a dissolution is to let the state settle what a church is worth, and in 1543 the state priced Tewkesbury Abbey at the weight of its lead. The townsmen paid it. Peter explains why such episodes are permitted at all: “That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth” (1Pe 1:7) is worth more than the thing tested. Paul warns that the assay is universal and public: “Every man's work shall be made manifest: for the day shall declare it” (1Co 3:13). What a town paid to keep a church standing was a disclosure of what it valued.
